old: Read this slowly into a recorder, speak it aloud, or learn its movement and use silent words if that comes easily. Choose one anchor—a sound, bodily contact, or your two-hand practice—and an opening phrase. Keep using the same anchor where the words refer to it. Pause between paragraphs; don’t read the delivery directions aloud.
new: Note: It may be useful to practice how you are going to read this into the recorder. You could either read it, or you could learn it. If you learn it, you might like to say some of the words in your head, silently. You will need to choose which of the three anchors you will use throughout – sound, bodily contact or two hands. You will also need to choose a phrase to use for the opening. Whenever the script says ‘the anchor’ use the one you have chosen. At the end of each paragraph pause for a few moments. Do not read out the instructions about how to read.

old: Let your eyes settle somewhere in the room, somewhere they can rest for a little while, and notice the difference between looking for something and letting what is already there come into view.
new: Allow your eyes to settle somewhere in the room.

old: There is a surface beneath you. Notice where you meet it … the contact, the pressure, whatever you can actually feel. And while you notice that, a sound may reach you, or a breath may draw your attention, without needing you to arrange either one.
new: As you notice where you are, notice the feel of it, the contact, and as you notice the contact a sound, a breath.

old: You can give this a little time.
new: There’s time to do this.

old: A thought about the day may still be here. A thought about whether you’re doing this properly may be here too. There is room to notice a thought and return to the anchor you chose, without finishing the thought first.
new: Perhaps there’s a thought there about something that has happened today, or a thought about doing this, but even if there is a thought there, is there a way of allowing your attention to be with the anchor?

old: And as you return, you may find one detail that holds your interest … something about the sound, or the contact, or that particular way of listening … and let attention stay with it long enough to become curious.
new: And in allowing your attention to be with the anchor, is there something about it that you can be interested in, a particular way of listening,

old: Perhaps you can give yourself the time you would give someone you care about who has begun to speak and hasn’t yet found the words. You can remain nearby, listening, without finishing their sentence for them.
new: Perhaps giving yourself as much time as you would if someone dear to you was trying to say something to you,

old: Let your chosen phrase come to mind now. Say it as an invitation, and notice how it is received.
new: Notice the receiving of the words of the phrase you have chosen.

old: As you continue, your eyes can close, soften, or stay open. Let that be a choice you make. Listening may deepen while a sound from the room remains available in the background.
new: You can close your eyes now if you like, or soften them, or keep them open, as you proceed. You choose. Perhaps as you listen your listening deepens, and yet in the background of your listening, a sound.

old: Count slowly from five to one. Give each number its own moment.
new: Counting slowly from 5 down to 1.

old: Five. Notice your chosen anchor again. Four. Let attention gather around what you find. Three. Leave a little space after the words. Two. Listen into that space, without preparing an answer. One. Stay here for a moment.
new: 5, perhaps noticing again your chosen anchor for today, 4, 3, 2, listening into the space, 1.

old: Bring your chosen concern lightly to mind, or remain with your wish for contact. Let it be present without rehearsing its whole story.
new: Bring to mind lightly the concern you have chosen to work with today. Or if you prefer, simply bring to mind the wish to come into contact.

old: What am I noticing now?
new: Perhaps you can notice what it is that you notice.

old: Give the response time to take its own form. It might be a sensation, a few words, an image, a feeling, or an impulse to move. There may be nothing clear yet.
new: Allow yourself some time to notice whatever it is that is coming to you, whether it is sensations, or words, or images, or feelings, or movements, or even if it is nothing.

old: Leave room to notice, with words or without them.
new: Allow yourself some time to notice this, with or without words.

old: Dishonest reframing declares that the problem was secretly good all along. I prefer questions that widen meaning without lying:
“What else might be true?” “What is this part trying to do for me?” “What would the Nurturer, the Protector, and the Leader each say about this?”
new: These reframe statements are dishonest because they make the problem into something that is good. Instead ask yourself: What else might be true? or What else could this be about? or How might this part reframe this? or How might my Nurturer reframe this? or How might my Protector reframe this? or How might my Leader reframe this? etc., etc.

old: Advertising, fear, craving, screens, tribe, resentment, authority, loneliness, and repetition are already training the mind. Self-hypnosis lets you practice from inside it: befriending the deeper layers, listening closely, and making adult choice more available.
new: Why learn Self Hypnosis? There are already a lot of forces that are out to train your mind. By learning to be able to train your own mind using self hypnosis, you will be befriending an aspect of you that up until now may have been unknown to you, thereby giving you a whole new area of choice as an adult.

old: Use self-hypnosis as a relationship with yourself. When the situation needs actual care, the guide shouldn’t become a substitute for it.
new: Remember that this is self hypnosis, it’s between you and you. If it doesn’t feel like it’s between you and you, this is probably not the right guide.

old: Get urgent help now for immediate danger, severe confusion, inability to keep yourself safe, or concerning physical symptoms such as chest pain or fainting. New or worsening suicidal thoughts, severe insomnia, mania-like or psychosis-like symptoms, or dissociation that disrupts functioning need prompt professional assessment, not a four-to-twelve-week practice schedule.
new: If you feel like you need help now for any reason (you’re in imminent danger, very confused, unsure of how to keep yourself safe, having physical symptoms like chest pain or fainting, etc.), please get help now. If you have symptoms that would benefit from professional help soon (new/worsening suicidal thoughts, aren’t sleeping enough, new/worsening mania or psychosis, dissociative symptoms that are affecting your ability to function, etc.) this is probably not the right guide; it’s unlikely that those things will go away in 4-12 weeks.

old: Don’t pry.
“Show me the capacity before the content.”
new: [Refrain] First show me the capacity And then show me the content

old: Sit up and open your eyes.
“What real action is this fantasy replacing?”
new: Sit up, open your eyes. What are you avoiding To do in reality By this fantasy?
